model:glm|title:glm models cut ai coding.content_excerpt: Revolut serves 80 million customers across 45 markets, and a secondary share sale that closed in July 2026 valued it at $115 billion, making it Europe's most valuable private company. It also, according to the man who runs its AI operations, now spends about one-tenth on AI coding tokens what it used to pay Anthropic and OpenAI. The blended cost of running self-hosted GLM models is 30 cents per million tokens, David Abitbol said on the AI Engineer podcast — and that single number is quietly rewriting how a regulated bank buys artificial intelligence. The striking part is not the discount. It is that Revolut reached it by doing less: fewer GPUs than the workload would seem to demand, less context than the models advertise, less precision than the hardware allows, and fewer permissions than an autonomous agent would want. Constraint, not capacity, turned out to be the lever. Revolut's numbers come from a sample of 2,000 engineers tracked over roughly a year, which makes them unusual — most enterprises deploying AI assistants have no clean before-and-after. The first rollout, Gemini in January 2025, delivered a 10% improvement in lead time and 20% in coding time. Abitbol credits the coding gain to engineers no longer digging through Stack Overflow and documentation. Claude Code was trialed around February 2025 and launched at scale in January 2026, but showed little measurable impact at first — and the cost raised eyebrows. Engineers were spending $1,000 to $10,000 a month with weak returns, so the rollout arrived with strict budget caps. Self-hosting open-source models from around April 2026 changed the picture. GLM 5.1 at that point delivered a 60% improvement in coding time and 70% in lead time. The asymmetry is the insight. The larger gain landed on lead time, not coding time, because writing code was never the bottleneck. "What we find is the bottleneck for engineering is not necessarily coding," Abitbol said. "You can save a lot of time not having to dig through your inbox or messing with Jira and Confluence." There is a second-order effect that does not show up in the table. When tokens are effectively unlimited, engineers stop rationing them — saving the expensive tool for the end of the quarter or the hardest task — and start using it on everything. Abitbol's posture now is blunt: open source is the priority, billing is flat with no month-to-month bill shock, and frontier models are the exception. story|title:a browser api for choosing a.content_excerpt: navigator.models is a proposed browser API for web apps that need a particular open-weight model on-device. A workflow built around one model may not work with another. Apps should be able to ask for the model they built and tested against, regardless of which browser someone uses. Web Models makes that request explicit. The page names a model ID. The browser runs that model or tells the page it can’t. There is no quiet fallback. The best model for scanning a receipt, transcribing audio, and searching documents may differ. A model ID lets a developer ask for the same model and release in any browser. Some models take gigabytes to download and plenty of memory to run. The browser can share their weights across sites, so every site does not need to download and store another copy. An app asks for a model, and the browser asks the user. They can see and revoke access for each site and model. The browser also keeps an eye on setup, execution, and resource limits. When someone searches their notes or documents, they should not have to send them to a model provider. Local inference can keep that data on-device and work offline when the model and content are already there. Your app picks the model and calls the API. The user grants access. The browser runs it. This is just illustrative JavaScript. <model-id> is a placeholder. Your app provides button , output , and showFallback() . The first access request has to start with a user gesture. This page does not run a model. For a one-off task, make a direct call. If you will use the model again, keep it in a session. Your app still owns the conversation history. Once access is granted, the browser tells you what that model supports. Vision, audio, tools, structured output, reasoning, and embeddings all depend on the model you chose. Each ID is tied to fixed weights, a tokenizer, and default input and generation settings. A changed release gets a new ID, so developers decide when to move to it. Shared catalogs, model retirement, and cross-browser compatibility tests are still open questions. Open an example to see the code. The model IDs are placeholders; replace them with the specific model IDs your app uses. story|title:gavel guided code review wit.content_excerpt: Review local Git changes in your browser with Claude Code or Codex . The gavel skill tells your agent to prepare a brief, explain its choices beside the code, and guide you through the diff. Large changes are split into focused reviews, so you have less context to hold in your head at once. Ask questions in threads, request revisions, and give each part a verdict. As a background task, I’ve been working for … longer than I’d like to admit on the task of adding authentication and authorization to PhotoStructure. The fourth (!!) dev spike was the charm—the first three attempts left me with a pretty solid set of specifications to guide the implementation. I wrote the db schema and the onboarding flow. Claude and Codex helped flesh out the implementation over several hundred sessions, coordinated with technical project plans . I reviewed every change before committing it. And it’s been a slog . It’s a given that authentication and authorization are going to be hard. But I felt like my reviewing approach kinda sucked had a lot of opportunity for improvement. It’s a bit of a PITA. My brain only has so many thinks it can think in a day. Any friction to giving the robot feedback, especially as your brain fades, can let “fuck it, ship it” creep in. I was explaining this to my wife during a walk, and realized that there was a better way. At a prior job at a Big Company, I helped interns get their PRs approved and merged by having them write a narrative around their diffs . This approach helps walk the reviewer through the PR, and is way better than the asciibetical sort order of staged diffs and a proposed git commit message that I’d been slogging through. The reviewer spends their limited cognitive mojo on judging the PR, not on basic orientation and background arcana. If the agent could write a “brief” for every review–just a sentence or three–and then add linked comments through the diffs to walk me through the changes, each review would be much simpler to digest and wrap my brain around. But, ugh, agents still work via a glorified chat interface. The Codex and Claude desktop apps, for example, each have a diff tool, but neither threads your comments. Juggling multiple issues simultaneously in one review is work . I’ve also seen the Codex diff viewer get confused and show irrelevant diffs from other worktrees. The Codex iOS app is supposed to show diffs, but that hasn’t worked for me, and the Claude iOS app doesn’t even have diffs afaict. I looked for an open sou
